content:
Quick answer: A good meal plan for arthritis follows the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean: vegetables and fruit at most meals, wholegrains, beans and lentils, oily fish at least once a week, olive or rapeseed oil, and less processed meat and sugar. Plan meals that are easy to prepare on bad days, batch cook on good days, and see a dietitian for advice on your own portions and needs.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS Eatwell Guide, NHS healthy eating tips, NICE NG100 and NICE NG226.

Knowing what to eat is one thing. Actually getting healthy meals on the table when your joints hurt and you are tired is another. A simple meal plan takes away daily decisions, makes shopping easier and means you can cook on good days and rest on bad ones. This guide gives you a seven-day plan using everyday UK food, a shopping list, and practical ways to make it work with arthritis.

The principles behind the plan

No diet has been proven to cure arthritis. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) says there is no strong evidence that diet changes help arthritis itself, but people can be encouraged to follow Mediterranean diet principles: more bread, fruit, vegetables and fish, less meat, and plant-oil-based products in place of butter and cheese. For osteoarthritis, NICE guidance (NG226) highlights weight management for people living with overweight or obesity.

This plan is built on the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean:

  • Fruit and vegetables: at least 5 portions a day, about a third of what you eat. Fresh, frozen, tinned and dried all count.
  • Starchy foods: just over a third of what you eat, ideally wholegrain or higher-fibre.
  • Protein: beans, pulses, fish, eggs and some meat. At least 2 portions of fish a week, 1 of them oily.
  • Dairy or alternatives: for protein and calcium, choosing lower-fat and lower-sugar options where possible.
  • Fats: small amounts of unsaturated oils such as olive and rapeseed oil.
  • Fluids: 6 to 8 cups or glasses a day.
  • Less often: foods high in fat, salt and sugar, and processed meats.

A note on portions and calories

This plan does not set calorie targets. The NHS gives a general guide that women need around 2,000 calories a day and men around 2,500, but needs vary with age, size and activity, and many people with arthritis are less active than average. If you want to lose or gain weight, or have other conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease, ask your GP for a referral to a registered dietitian, who can tailor portions to you. A simple visual guide is to fill about half your plate with vegetables or salad, a quarter with a starchy food and a quarter with protein.

The 7-day meal plan

DayBreakfastLunchEvening meal
MondayPorridge with milk, frozen berries and ground flaxseedLentil and vegetable soup (batch) with wholemeal breadBaked salmon, new potatoes with skins, peas and broccoli
TuesdayWholemeal toast with peanut butter and bananaLeftover salmon mixed with salad leaves, tomatoes and a wholemeal wrapChickpea and spinach curry (batch) with brown rice
WednesdayPlain yoghurt with oats, apple and walnutsJacket potato with baked beans and a side saladChicken and vegetable traybake (peppers, red onion, courgette) with olive oil and herbs, with couscous
ThursdayScrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with tomatoesLeftover chickpea curry with a wholemeal pittaWholewheat pasta with a tomato, lentil and vegetable sauce (batch), and a side salad
FridayOvernight oats with grated apple and cinnamonSardines on toast with cherry tomatoes and cucumberFish pie topped with mashed potato (shop-bought fish pie mix makes it easier), with green beans
SaturdayVegetable omelette with wholemeal toastHummus, falafel and salad in a wholemeal wrapBean and vegetable chilli (batch) with brown rice and plain yoghurt
SundayWholegrain cereal with milk and sliced fruitLeftover chilli in a jacket potatoRoast chicken with roast potatoes (in a little rapeseed oil), carrots, cabbage and gravy

Snacks if you need them: a piece of fruit, a small handful of unsalted nuts, plain yoghurt, carrot sticks and hummus, or wholegrain crackers with cheese.

Drinks: water, tea, coffee and milk all count towards your fluids. The NHS suggests limiting fruit juice and smoothies to a combined 150ml a day.

Why this plan works for arthritis

  • Oily fish twice a week (salmon on Monday, sardines on Friday) provides long-chain omega-3 fats, which have some evidence of benefit in rheumatoid arthritis and support heart health.
  • Beans and lentils appear most days, adding protein and fibre at low cost.
  • Wholegrains such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread provide fibre and steady energy.
  • Calcium from milk, yoghurt, cheese and sardines supports bone health.
  • Little processed meat and few sugary foods, in line with NHS advice.
  • Leftovers are built in, so you cook less often.

Batch-cooking plan for good days

On a day when your joints are less painful, spend an hour or two making three big batches. Then you only need to reheat on most days.

  1. Lentil and vegetable soup: onion, carrots, celery, red lentils, tinned tomatoes and stock. Freeze in single portions.
  2. Chickpea and spinach curry: onion, garlic, ginger paste, curry paste, tinned chickpeas, tinned tomatoes and frozen spinach.
  3. Bean and vegetable chilli or lentil pasta sauce: tinned kidney beans or lentils, tinned tomatoes, frozen mixed peppers and onions, and spices.

Tips to save your joints:

  • Use frozen chopped onions, peppers and vegetables, and jars of garlic and ginger paste, so there is little chopping.
  • Use a lightweight saucepan or slow cooker, and sit on a perching stool while you stir.
  • Ladle food into containers rather than lifting heavy pans to pour.
  • Label portions with the name and date, and use them within the time recommended for frozen food.
  • Pace yourself: split the cooking across two short sessions if you need to.

For a printable version of the basics, see our anti-inflammatory shopping list.

Swaps for painful or exhausting days

Planned mealLow-effort swap
Baked salmon with vegetablesMicrowave salmon fillet pouch, microwave rice and frozen veg steamed in the bag
Chicken traybakeReady-roasted chicken with a bag of salad and a wholemeal roll
Fish pieTinned mackerel on wholemeal toast with tomatoes
Any home-cooked evening mealA portion of frozen batch-cooked soup, curry or chilli
Roast dinnerSupermarket ready meal with extra frozen vegetables. Check the label for salt

It is fine to rely on convenience foods sometimes. A ready meal with added vegetables is a better choice than skipping a meal.

Adapting the plan

  • Vegetarian: swap fish and chicken for eggs, tofu, beans, lentils or Quorn. Include walnuts and ground flaxseed for plant omega-3.
  • Vegan: use fortified soya alternatives and plan for vitamin B12, iodine, calcium and vitamin D.
  • Gout: some foods, including red meat, offal and some seafood, are higher in purines. Ask your GP or a dietitian how to adapt the plan.
  • Weight loss: keep the same pattern but adjust portions of starchy foods and fats, and limit snacks. NICE says any amount of weight loss is likely to help osteoarthritis.
  • Small appetite: eat little and often, and include protein at each meal. See a dietitian if you are losing weight without trying.
  • Jaw arthritis or swallowing difficulty: choose soft options such as soups, fish pie, scrambled eggs and porridge, and ask for a speech and language therapy assessment if swallowing is difficult.
  • Warfarin: keep your intake of green leafy vegetables fairly steady from week to week, and tell your anticoagulant clinic if you make big diet changes.

Some people notice certain foods seem to affect their symptoms. Our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms explains how to test this without cutting out whole food groups.

Make your own plan: a weekly planner

Once you have tried the plan above, you may want to build your own around foods you enjoy. Copy this planner onto paper or into your phone. Fill in your good days first (for batch cooking) and plan the easiest meals for days when you have appointments, work or usually feel worse.

A quick weekly check: have you included oily fish at least once, beans or lentils on several days, wholegrains most days, and fruit or vegetables at most meals? If so, your plan follows the same principles as the one above.

Storing and reheating leftovers safely

Batch cooking only works if leftovers are stored safely. Cool cooked food quickly, put it in the fridge or freezer once cool, and reheat until steaming hot all the way through. Only reheat food once. Defrost frozen portions in the fridge or microwave rather than on the worktop. The Food Standards Agency has more detailed food safety advice.

Getting help with food

If shopping and cooking are becoming too difficult, there are options. Supermarket online deliveries, frozen meal delivery services and community meal services can help, and a social care needs assessment from your local council may include help with meals. An occupational therapist can suggest equipment to make cooking easier. See our guide to meal delivery and help with food.

Want a longer plan?

Once you are comfortable with this week, try our 14-day Mediterranean plan for more variety, or our breakfast guide for easy morning ideas.

When to see a dietitian

A meal plan like this is a general starting point. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral to a registered dietitian if you want help to lose or gain weight, have diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, gout or food allergies, follow a vegan diet, or have lost weight without trying. Dietitians can tailor portions and food choices to your needs.

When to get medical help

Do not change your prescribed arthritis medicines because of diet changes. See your GP if you lose weight without trying, have ongoing digestive symptoms, or are struggling to eat enough. Speak to a pharmacist before starting supplements, especially if you take warfarin or another anticoagulant, methotrexate or NSAIDs. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a special meal plan for arthritis?

No meal plan has been proven to treat arthritis. A plan based on the NHS Eatwell Guide with a Mediterranean-style lean is the best-supported approach and is good for your heart and weight.

How many calories should I eat?

The NHS gives a general guide of around 2,000 calories a day for women and 2,500 for men, but needs vary. A registered dietitian can advise on what is right for you.

Can I follow this plan if I have gout?

Much of it is suitable, but some foods are higher in purines. Ask your GP or a dietitian to help you adapt it.

Is it OK to use ready meals and frozen food?

Yes. Frozen vegetables, tinned fish and beans are nutritious, and a ready meal with extra vegetables is better than skipping a meal. Check labels for salt.

How do I eat healthily when cooking is painful?

Batch cook on good days, use frozen and pre-prepared ingredients, sit while you cook, and keep easy standbys such as tinned fish, eggs and microwave grains.

Will this meal plan help me lose weight?

It is based on healthy, filling foods, which can help. For weight loss, portion sizes matter; a dietitian or NHS weight management service can help you set realistic goals.
